steps.description: Native **ETH** and generic yield-bearing tokens are handled in the codebase through two tiny **interfaces**.  We will look at what each interface exposes and then see real **call-sites** so you can recognise the wrapping / pricing pattern across the code.
The Wrapped-ETH interface extends ERC-20 but only adds the two functions that bridge between native ETH and the ERC-20 world.

- `deposit()` – payable, consumes `msg.value`, mints `WETH` 1:1.
- `withdraw(amount)` – burns `amount` of `WETH` held by the caller, then sends the same amount of native `ETH` back.
These two functions are all that is required anywhere else in the system to turn `ETH` into an **ERC-20** balance and back again.
AlchemistETHVault accepts WETH, then **unwraps** it immediately so it can keep a pure-ETH balance.  Note the call to `IWETH.withdraw`.
In tests a user first calls `IWETH.deposit{value: amount}()` to obtain WETH before approving and sending it to the vault – showing the other side of the wrap/unwrap pair.
With that the life-cycle of **ETH** in the protocol is clear: external users wrap using `deposit()`, internal contracts unwrap again with `withdraw()` when they only need the native coin.
The second micro-interface standardises valuation for any interest-bearing or derivative token.

`price()` is a pure/view call that returns how many **underlying tokens** one whole `yield token` is currently worth (scaled to the `underlying`’s **decimals**). Every concrete `yield token` just needs to expose this read-only number.
Adapters wrap a concrete yield token and forward the `price()` call, enforcing the unified API.
Core logic then relies on that adapter to convert between yield-token balances and underlying value using the returned price, without needing to know which concrete token is underneath.

Key takeaways:
- `IWETH` is the one-stop bridge between native ETH and ERC-20 form; contracts call only `deposit()` / `withdraw()`.
- `IYieldToken` exposes a single `price()` so every part of the protocol can value very different yield assets through an identical interface.
- Adapters and vaults import these interfaces where they need wrapping or valuation, keeping the rest of the system agnostic to asset specifics.
